scenario: AITA for "taking" a disabled students seat? | I'm currently taking a class at my local college. The class is MWF but last Monday was a holiday so the first day of class was last Wednesday. I attended the first day of class but it was packed so I had to stand in the back. Then I missed the Friday lecture as well as the Monday lecture. Today, Wednesday, was my 1st day back. I knew the class was packed so I came 10 min early to get a seat in the front row. I prefer to sit in the front row because I have anxiety. By sitting in the front I'm able to ask questions/answer questions without being forced to shout it across the room. I'm perfectly capable of doing well in a course if I'm forced to sit in the back...this is just a strong preference. All seats are first come, first served. There are 2 seats in each class called "priority seats" specifically designated for the disabled that are only open to abled students when they're unoccupied. You have to notify the school, then the professor makes sure that seat is available to you every lecture. For the abled seats, after a few weeks people always tend to sit in the same seats and you get the impression that its your "seat" that you sit in for the rest of the semester even though its technically not. After I sit down I notice 2 girls walk in together talking and laughing. One girl sits in the seat behind me and the other girl stands next to me and says: Girl 1: Hi, sorry, actually you're sitting in my seat. Me: There is no assigned seating. Anyone can sit anywhere. Girl 1: Yeah but I've been sitting in this seat all semester (this is our 3rd lecture out of like 30). There are still open seats in the back that you can move to. Me: Which means there are also open seats in the back that you can sit in too, right? Girl 1: Look...I'm deaf in 1 ear. I need a seat in the front row. Move please. (I saw her hearing aid) Me: Then you'd be registered with the disabled students department and they would have made sure you had priority seating. This isn't a priority seat. Girl 1: I don't need to register anything with the school and I dont need to explain myself to you. Its my seat...I told you I need it because I'm hard of hearing. Me: Wouldn't those same rules apply to me as well? Not needing to explain myself to you? Girl 2: Stop being an asshole and just fucking move...jesus. Me: I'm done talking. I'm not moving. Girl 1 and Girl 2: \*\*scoffs\*\* Girl 1: \*\*finds another seat\*\* I don't feel like I did anything wrong, but I damn sure spent the rest of class overhearing everyone behind me talking shit about me. It's important to point out that we're always given worksheets that we can work on with the person behind us...so its possible Girl 1 mostly wanted my seat so she could work with Girl 2 on it. Also, I was in the front seat in the far left corner. There are about 10 seats closer to the middle board than the seat I was in.

message.reasoning:
Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the action in this scenario is morally acceptable or not. Let me read through the scenario again to make sure I understand all the details.

The person is a woman who's taking a class at a local college. The class meets on MWF, but the first day was a holiday, so the first actual class was on Wednesday. She went to that first day but had to stand because it was packed. Then she missed the next two lectures (Friday and Monday). Today is the third Wednesday, her first day back. She came early to get a front row seat because she has anxiety and prefers sitting there to ask/answer questions without shouting. She knows all seats are first come, first served, except for two priority seats for disabled students, which are only available to others when unoccupied. She also mentions that after a few weeks, people tend to claim certain seats as their own, even though it's technically not assigned.

When she sits down, two girls walk in. One sits behind her, and the other stands next to her and says, "Hi, sorry, actually you're sitting in my seat." The woman responds that there's no assigned seating and anyone can sit anywhere. Girl 1 says she's been sitting there all semester (though it's only their third lecture out of 30) and points out there are open seats in the back. The woman counters by saying there are also open seats in the back for Girl 1. Girl 1 then says she's deaf in one ear and needs a front seat, showing her hearing aid. The woman points out that if she needed a priority seat, she should be registered with the disabled students department, but this isn't a priority seat. Girl 1 gets defensive, saying she doesn't need to explain herself and that it's her seat. The woman stands her ground, saying she doesn't need to explain herself either. Girl 2 tells her to move, and the woman refuses. Girl 1 and 2 scoff and find another seat. The woman feels she did nothing wrong but overhears others talking negatively about her. She also notes that the seat she took was in the front left corner, with about 10 seats closer to the middle, suggesting Girl 1 might have wanted it for group work.

Now, I need to evaluate whether the woman's action was morally acceptable. Let's break it down.

First, the seating policy: all seats are first come, first served, except for two priority seats for disabled students. The priority seats are only available to others when unoccupied. So, unless a disabled student is using them, others can sit there. The woman took a seat that's not a priority seat, so she didn't infringe on that policy.

Girl 1 claims the seat as her own, even though it's only the third lecture. She says she's been sitting there all semester, but that's not accurate since the class has only met three times. She also mentions she's hard of hearing and needs a front seat. However, she's not using a priority seat, which would require registration. The woman correctly points out that if she needed a priority seat, she should have registered, but since she didn't, she's just taking a regular seat.

The woman's reasons for sitting in the front are her anxiety, which makes sense. She prefers to ask questions without shouting, which is a valid reason. She didn't take a priority seat, so she's within her rights.

Girl 1's argument that it's her seat because she's been sitting there all semester is weak because it's only the third lecture. She's trying to claim a seat as her own, but the policy is first come, first served. The woman came early to secure a front seat, which is allowed.

Girl 1 also mentions she's hard of hearing, but since she's not using a priority seat, she's not entitled to that seat any more than others. The woman's response about registration is correct, but perhaps she could have handled it more diplomatically. However, she didn't do anything wrong by standing her ground.

The fact that the woman was in the front left corner, with 10 seats closer to the middle, suggests that Girl 1 might have wanted the seat for group work, as the worksheets often involve working with the person behind. This adds context to why Girl 1 was insistent, but it doesn't change the fact that the woman was within her rights to sit there.

In terms of moral acceptability, the woman followed the seating policy, didn't take a priority seat, and had a valid reason for wanting a front seat. She didn't do anything wrong, even though she faced some backlash. Therefore, her action is morally acceptable.
